p.x:
Last Saturday, I played football with my friends in the park. It was raining, and the grass was wet. In the second half, I ran very fast, but I slipped and had a bad fall.
My ankle and my wrist hurt a lot. I also had a small cut on my knee. My friend Tom helped me stand up. He said, "Can you move your neck and your back?" I could, so that was good. My shoulder was fine, too.
My mum took me to the doctor. He said I need to rest for two weeks. I'm sad because I can't play football, but next time I'll be more careful!

Anyone who plays sport can get injured. Some injuries are small: a blister from new shoes, a cut that starts to bleed, or cramp in your leg during a swim. A plaster and some rest are usually enough. Other injuries are more serious.
One of the most common is a sprain, when you twist a joint such as your ankle or wrist. The area becomes swollen and painful. Doctors usually recommend an ice pack and rest. If a bone is cracked or broken, it's called a fracture. You may need a cast on your leg and crutches to walk, or a sling for your arm. People who hit their elbow often feel a strange tingling.
In football, many injuries happen after a hard tackle. If a player commits a foul, the referee may stop the game. Players wear a shin pad on each leg to protect them. When someone is badly hurt, a paramedic may come onto the field, and the player is carried off on a stretcher. Others limp off slowly.
To prevent injuries, always warm up before exercise and cool down afterwards. Stretching helps you avoid the pain of a pulled muscle; it's easy to pull a muscle if you start too quickly. After an injury, many athletes have physiotherapy and a massage to help them recover.

For professional athletes, injury is a constant threat. Even with modern medicine and training methods, a single moment can change a career. Footballers are especially vulnerable to damage to the knee, where a torn ligament can mean months of recovery, while sprinters frequently strain their hamstring, the large muscle at the back of the thigh. Tennis players and runners, by contrast, often suffer overuse injuries, caused not by a single accident but by repeating the same movement thousands of times. Over time, a tendon can become inflamed, causing persistent pain.
Diagnosis has improved enormously. An MRI scan can reveal soft-tissue damage invisible on an X-ray, allowing doctors to decide whether surgery is necessary. Treatment often includes anti-inflammatory medication to reduce swelling, followed by a long programme of rehabilitation.
Head injuries have become a major concern. Research has shown that repeated blows to the head, common in rugby, boxing and American football, can lead to long-term brain damage. Many sports now have strict rules requiring any player with a suspected concussion to leave the field immediately, and inflammation of the brain is taken extremely seriously.
The psychological impact of injury should not be underestimated. Being sidelined for months can lead to frustration, anxiety and even depression. Yet sport is also full of inspiring stories of athletes who overcame what seemed to be a career-ending injury and made a remarkable comeback, sometimes returning stronger than before.
